items.question: Why is the opponent's appeal to conceptual construction refuted in the case of taking food?
premises: Hungry people take food and so on in order to eat.
They do so without the mediation of pervasion and other inferential steps.
The opponent claims such cognition is mere conceptual construction.
items.inference: Because the act occurs without inferential mediation, the opponent's claim that it is conceptual construction is thereby refuted.
items.plain_english: People take food to eat without any intervening inference of pervasion or the like; therefore what the opponents call mere conceptual construction is already answered and refuted.

items.question: In well-practiced cases, what need is there for cognition pervaded by conceptual construction?
premises: In well-practiced cases there is awareness of pervasion whose nature is invariable concomitance.
The opponent proposes cognition pervaded by conceptual construction to explain such cases.
The author rejects that proposed mechanism.
items.inference: Since the awareness is already established through practice, there is no need to posit cognition pervaded by conceptual construction.
items.plain_english: In matters that have become well practiced, where awareness of invariable pervasion is already present, what use is there for a cognition pervaded by conceptual construction? We do not accept that.

rows.grounds: what is absent due to speed

items.question: Does the swift arising of the cognition justify inferring hidden conceptual construction?
premises: The cognition arises so swiftly that it is not clearly noticed.
The opponent infers from this lack of noticing that conceptual construction is present.
The author presents this inference as the opponent's position.
items.inference: The opponent concludes that the unnoticed swift cognition is itself conceptual construction, but this rests only on its not being noticed.
items.plain_english: Because this cognition arises very quickly, it is not clearly noticed; so the opponent infers that it must be conceptual construction. That is the move being stated here.

items.question: What fault does the author find in the logicians who defend this position?
premises: The opponents are blinded by attachment to their own side.
They repeatedly forget even what they themselves have accepted.
They pride themselves on being logicians.
items.inference: Their attachment to their own position makes them inconsistent with their own admitted doctrines.
items.plain_english: Alas, these people who fancy themselves logicians, blinded by loyalty to their own side, have begun again and again to forget even what they themselves have accepted.

rows.grounds: nature of cognition in opponent's view

items.question: What do the opponents themselves hold about how cognition manifests its object?
premises: According to the opponent, every cognition ends in a single moment.
According to the opponent, cognition manifests its object by the mere fact of arising.
This doctrine is admitted by the opponents themselves.
items.inference: On the opponent's own view, a cognition reveals its object at the very moment of its arising, without needing further duration.
items.plain_english: For in your own view, every cognition lasts only a moment and manifests its object simply by arising.

items.question: If cognition lasts only a moment, what follows about swift manifestation?
premises: Swift manifesting capacity is not anything beyond a single moment.
Every cognition, on the opponent's view, operates within that momentary arising.
No extra duration is available to distinguish swift from non-swift manifestation.
items.inference: Therefore, in truth, every cognition would have to be counted as swiftly manifesting.
items.plain_english: If swift manifestation means nothing more than what happens in a moment, then in truth every cognition would be swiftly manifesting.

items.question: What problematic consequence follows if momentariness makes all cognition unnoticed or extended?
premises: If momentariness alone explains non-noticing, that consequence would apply everywhere among things.
Alternatively, one might appeal to unbroken seeing over a longer time.
The opponent must account for cognition that ranges over a longer duration.
items.inference: The opponent's momentary model either makes non-noticing universal or fails to explain cognition that spans a longer time.
uncertainties: The exact syntactic break between the two halves is compressed; the contrast is read from atha and the genitive plural.
items.plain_english: Then non-noticing would occur everywhere among all things; or else, in the case of unbroken seeing, what is known would have to range over a longer time.

items.question: If an object is manifested by mere arising, how can arising alone explain its clarity?
premises: The opponent holds that an object is manifested by the mere birth of cognition.
The opponent also holds that cognition becomes clear in its object because of arising alone.
Both claims rely on the same momentary arising.
items.inference: If mere arising is sufficient for manifestation and clarity, the opponent must explain how differences in clarity or timing arise.
items.plain_english: Then even on that view the object is manifested by mere arising; and if clarity of the object is also due simply to arising, that same fact must explain everything.

rows.grounds: refers to the cognition or clarity

items.question: How can a swifter experience create difference if cognition is already self-luminous?
premises: The opponent treats a swifter experience as what makes a difference.
The opponent also says cognition is self-luminous, though possibly related to grasping.
A self-luminous cognition does not obviously need speed to differentiate it.
items.inference: If cognition is self-luminous, the appeal to a swifter experience cannot by itself explain the relevant difference.
uncertainties: grahāpekṣaṃ is read as 'dependent on grasping' in the opponent's framework; the exact polemical target is compressed.
items.plain_english: How can the fact that the experience is quicker make a difference, if that cognition is said to be self-luminous, even while being related to grasping?

items.question: Can temporal duration, like lightning or a lamp, explain cognitive difference?
premises: A cognition might serve as a means elsewhere, like lightning or a lamp.
Lightning and lamps differ by lasting briefly or longer.
The opponent may use that temporal difference to explain cognitive difference.
items.inference: Even if temporal duration appears to make a difference in such analogies, that does not yet show how momentary cognitions yield the required unified awareness.
items.plain_english: If it becomes a means elsewhere, like lightning or a lamp, then the difference between lasting long or briefly may appear right there as a basis for difference.

items.question: Why does repeated clarity not support the opponent's account of inference?
premises: In inferences, the grasping of pervasion and related factors does not recur as a newly noticed event each time.
If it became clear again and again, that repeated clarification would be noticed.
Such repeated noticing is not what actually occurs in ordinary inference.
items.inference: Because inferential grasping does not become repeatedly clear in a noticeable way, the opponent cannot explain inference by repeated momentary clarifications.
items.plain_english: And in inferences the grasping of pervasion and so on does not become clear again and again in such a way that it would be separately noticed.

items.question: How can a series of successive cognitions produce the manifestation of a single object?
premises: Inferential cognition may involve a series of successive cognitions, such as smoke and so on.
Each member of that series may arise clearly.
Inference requires the manifestation of one unified object or conclusion.
items.inference: A merely successive series of clear cognitions cannot by itself account for the manifestation of one unified object.
items.plain_english: Moreover, even if a clear series of successive cognitions of smoke and so on arises, how could that produce the manifestation of a single thing?

items.question: Can a final connecting cognition unify earlier cognitions if it is itself distinct?
premises: The opponent may propose a final connecting cognition to unify the series.
That final cognition is, on the same theory, distinct like the earlier cognitions.
A distinct momentary cognition faces the same problem of separation.
items.inference: A final connecting cognition cannot unify the series if it is just another distinct momentary cognition.
items.plain_english: If one says the final connecting cognition will do this, that too is distinct and just like the earlier cognitions—so how could it unify them in that way?

items.question: How can a final cognition connect earlier cognitions if they no longer exist?
premises: The opponent claims the final cognition connects the earlier series of cognitions.
On momentarism, earlier cognitions are no longer existent when the final cognition arises.
Connection requires something available to be connected.
items.inference: If the earlier cognitions have perished and are non-existent, their connection by a later cognition is not possible.
items.plain_english: If that final cognition is supposed to connect the earlier series of cognitions, but those earlier cognitions no longer exist, then no connection is possible once they have perished.

items.question: Can memory connect cognitions if there is no underlying experience to ground it?
premises: The opponent may propose memory as the connection between cognitions.
Memory requires some prior experience.
On the opponent's momentary model, the needed experience is not available as a unifying ground.
items.inference: Memory cannot supply the required connection if there is no genuine experience available to ground it.
items.plain_english: If one says that memory itself is the connection between cognitions, how could that memory arise at all in the absence of experience?

items.question: Why cannot awareness experience cognitions on the opponent's own momentary view?
premises: The opponent holds that two cognitions do not exist simultaneously.
Experience of a cognition by awareness would require a relation not available within that restriction.
The opponent's own doctrine blocks simultaneous pairing of cognitions.
items.inference: Given the opponent's denial of simultaneous cognitions, an experience of cognitions by awareness does not fit their system.
items.plain_english: And in your view there is no pair of cognitions existing simultaneously; so an experience of cognitions by awareness does not fit anywhere in that system.

items.question: Under what condition is the cognition-known relation observed, and when is it impossible?
premises: The relation of cognition and known is observed when two factors abide simultaneously.
Successive factors arise in prior and later form and are opposed in that way.
The opponent's model relies on such successive arising.
items.inference: The cognition-known relation cannot be established between successively arising, mutually opposed factors.
items.plain_english: The relation of cognition and its object is observed only where two factors stand together at the same time, not where they arise successively as earlier and later and are therefore opposed.

items.question: What kind of knowing is present even in cognition that follows pervasion?
premises: Some cognition appears to be preceded by manifestation following pervasion.
The preceding argument has undermined a merely sequential account of such cognition.
The author offers a positive characterization of that cognition.
items.inference: Even cognition that follows pervasion is, at its core, a non-sequential knowing akin to direct perception.
items.plain_english: Therefore, even the cognition that seems to be preceded by a manifestation following pervasion is, in that very case, a non-sequential knowing of a directly perceptual kind.

items.question: What analogy illustrates immediate perceptual knowing after waking from deep sleep?
premises: A person awakened suddenly from deep sleep has eyes just beginning to open.
That person acts to remove the dimness affecting the appearance of things.
The analogy is used to clarify immediate knowing.
items.inference: The waking person’s situation illustrates a direct apprehension that is not constructed through sequential inference.
items.plain_english: Just as someone suddenly awakened from deep sleep, with eyes just opening, acts to remove the dimness in the appearance of things, taking them directly...

items.question: What does the waking analogy show about ordinary inferential self-awareness?
premises: The person awakened from sleep rubs the eyes and does similar actions.
That person does not think, 'I am inferring these things.'
The same point applies to the disputed case of inference.
items.inference: Immediate practical cognition does not present itself as an inferential process, so the disputed cognition should be understood similarly.
items.plain_english: While rubbing the eyes and so on, that person does not think, 'I am inferring these things.' Let the same be understood in this case as well.

items.question: What does the momentary confusion after deep sleep illustrate about awareness?
premises: One who rises from the delusion of deep sleep may momentarily forget himself.
In that same moment he may also forget where he is.
This forgetting is temporary and occurs at the threshold of waking.
items.inference: The analogy shows that awareness can be temporarily veiled without ceasing to be the underlying ground of recognition.
items.plain_english: And just as someone whose vision has just emerged from the delusion of deep sleep may, for that moment, forget himself and the place he is in...

items.question: What restores self-recognition after the momentary confusion of waking?
premises: After initial confusion, effort gathers and clear seeing awakens.
The person then recognizes, 'I am that one.'
This recognition is grounded in awareness itself.
items.inference: Self-recognition arises from awareness in the ultimate sense, not from a merely sequential construction.
items.plain_english: Then, when his own clear seeing is awakened through gathered effort, he recognizes, 'I am that one,' and in the ultimate sense this comes from awareness itself.

items.question: Who is the ultimate agent behind the concealment and revelation of awareness?
premises: The processes of forgetting and recognition occur within awareness.
The Lord Bhairava is consciousness in nature.
By his freedom he conceals and reveals his own form.
items.inference: The alternation of concealment and revelation in cognition is ultimately the free activity of Bhairava, whose nature is consciousness.
items.plain_english: In all of this, the Lord Bhairava, whose very nature is consciousness, freely conceals and reveals his own form.

rows.grounds: of the subject or Lord's manifestation

items.question: How do ignorance and knowledge arise from the Lord's concealment and revelation?
premises: Bhairava freely conceals and reveals his own form.
Concealment corresponds to ignorance and revelation corresponds to knowledge.
The knowledge that arises appears with clarity.
items.inference: Ignorance and knowledge arise according to the Lord's concealment and revelation, and the resulting knowledge is clear and directly evident to all.
items.plain_english: To that extent ignorance arises, and knowledge arises; and that knowledge, by its clarity, should be understood as directly evident to all.
